title: The old new commandment (1 John 2:1–11)
hookLine: whoever hates his brother walks in darkness

lines: HE SEEMS TO CHANGE HIS MIND.
THE SAME WORDS, OLD AND NEW.
cards: Is it old or new? The writer of First John can't seem to decide, and that's the point. Within two verses he says, I'm not writing you a new commandment, it's an old one.
Then, right away: actually, it is new. It sounds like a man changing his mind mid-sentence. It isn't.
Ask a couple married for decades: the same words, I love you, can be very old and brand new at once. Today, the commandment that is both.

teach.b: He starts tenderly: "My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous."
An advocate stands beside you in court and speaks for you. Then a simple test: how do we know we know God? We keep his commandments, not just say we do.
Then the riddle: "Brethren, I write no new commandment unto you, but an old commandment which ye had from the beginning." Which old commandment? Love.

It runs back through the Torah: "love thy neighbour as thyself," in Leviticus. It's what his readers heard from the very beginning of their faith. Then he flips it: "Again, a new commandment I write unto you."
New, because in John's Gospel, at the Last Supper, Jesus says, "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another."
New, because now it has a face: love as he loved. And new, the writer says, "because the darkness is past, and the true light now shineth." It's dawn: something old seen in fresh light.
Then the hard edge: "He that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now."

teach.h: HATRED BLINDS THE ONE WHO HATES.
teach.b: Whoever hates walks in darkness and doesn't know where he's going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.
Hatred doesn't only hurt the other person; it takes away your own sight. Love is how you see where you're going.

how: Christians remember the new commandment especially on Maundy Thursday, whose name is usually traced to the Latin mandatum, commandment, and many churches read 1 John 2 when teaching about love within the community.

games.q: what's inside 1 John 2:1–11 — tap the pairs.
p: love one another, as he loved
is in darkness even until now

s: the writer contradicts himself about old and new
it's both: old as the Torah's call to love, new in Christ and in the dawning light.
the letter says hatred blinds the one who hates
an advocate is someone who speaks for you
the writer says Jesus Christ is our advocate with the Father.

games.q: someone says, I'm in the light, I know God, but they can't stand their brother. what does the letter say?
o: fine, faith is between you and God.
they are in darkness even until now.
games.why: "He that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now."

practice: Think of someone you hold something against, a small irritation or an old hurt, and notice what happens in your chest as you picture them.
Ask quietly what this grudge has kept you from seeing, about them, about you, about the way forward, without trying to fix it now. If you pray, pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Advocate. First John's name for Christ with the Father: someone who stands beside you in court and speaks for you when you sin.

orig.note: Greek: advocate, one called alongside. the same word John's Gospel uses for the Holy Spirit, the Comforter.

carryVoice: Your line: walk in the light. An old command, in a new dawn. Day six hundred eighty-three, done.
